html:
On 21 October 1972 the government of Siad Barre made a Latin alphabet the official script of the Somali language, ending years of debate between Latin, Arabic and the local Osmanya script.

Somali had a rich oral poetry but no agreed way of writing, and the state ran on English, Italian and Arabic. The new script, designed by the linguist Shire Jama Ahmed and others, uses letters such as c and x for sounds of Somali.

In 1974 and 1975 schools closed and students were sent to the countryside to teach herders to read, and literacy rose sharply, although the gains were later lost in the civil war. Somali is now written in the Latin script across the diaspora and online, a lasting result of Siad Barre's rule.
sum: On 21 October 1972 the government of Siad Barre made a Latin alphabet the official script of the Somali language, ending years of debate between Latin, Arabic and the local Osmanya script.
